ticket-runner <version> run <runId> · <duration> · <credential>

  merged   #3 Run: drain the Frontier (PR #12)
  noted    #8 comment · from #3 implement · the CLI help drifts from the README
  handed   #5 Fix Stage with a single retry · verify · 1 unmet
  noted    #31 new · from #5 fix · nothing cleans up abandoned worktrees
  skipped  #7 no-criteria
  skipped  #9 blocked

Frontier empty.

The verb is padded to nine columns so the Ticket numbers line up. A Run that
took no Ticket prints `  nothing to do` in place of the rows.

`<credential>` is what the Run's Stages were billed to: `subscription`, the
Claude login, or `API key`, the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` the Host exports, for a Run
started with `--api-key`. A subscription Run starts its Stages without that
key, whatever the Host exports.

`<version>` is the Version the Run ran (ADR-0007): the number alone from an
installed copy, and the number, the commit and a `dirty` mark from a development
checkout — `0.4.0`, `0.4.0+331d79c`, `0.4.0+331d79c.dirty`. Every stamp of one
Run says the same thing, and `.ticket-runner/runs/<runId>/version.txt` says it
again beside the transcripts.

A Run whose Version is below the highest one published on GitHub gains a line
above that header, which is also the first thing it logged hours earlier:

A newer Version is out: 0.5.0, and this is 0.4.0 — upgrade with `npm install -g ticket-runner`.
ticket-runner <version> run <runId> · <duration> · <credential>

  merged   #3 Run: drain the Frontier (PR #12)

Frontier empty.

Nothing is printed where this copy is the latest Version, where it is above it —
a development checkout runs a commit past the Version it reports, and is
compared by number only — or where GitHub could not be asked at all. No answer
is an answer, and none of them stops a Run.

The rows are in the order the Tickets ended, which is the order they were
claimed in only for a Run with one Lane. A Run with more than one has several
Tickets in flight at once, and each takes as long as its own Stages take.

`released` is a Ticket the rate limit or a transient API failure stopped
mid-flight — an API error with a 5xx status or none, after the CLI had given up
retrying it — or, on a Run started with `--api-key`, the key running out of
budget: its Claim was undone, and the State file it has been
keeping since it was claimed says where the next Run resumes it from. Nobody has to do anything about it, which is
why it is not `handed`. It stops the Run filling Lanes, so no Ticket is claimed
after it; the Lanes still busy finish what they hold, and whatever they end as
has its row after the `released` one:

ticket-runner <version> run <runId> · <duration> · <credential>

  released #6 Rebase conflict resolution · rate limit at implement
  merged   #3 Run: drain the Frontier (PR #12)

Rate limited · resets 2026-09-20 03:40 UTC.

The reset time is the one the CLI's rejecting `rate_limit_event` gave, in UTC to
the minute like a Stop's clock time, with the date because a weekly limit can
reset days later. The Run does not wait for it: a human or an Operator starts
the next one. A Run no event told the time ends `Rate limited.`, and one a
transient API failure stopped says which it was and nothing of when:

  released #6 Rebase conflict resolution · API failure at verify

API failure.

The rate limit is the subscription's on a subscription Run. On a Run started
with `--api-key` it is the API's, and is named so: its row reads `API rate
limit` and its last line `API rate limited.`, with the reset time where a Stage
was told one.

A Stage of an `--api-key` Run that ends on a 400 whose message names the credit
balance or the workspace's API usage limits is out of API budget: the key's
organization is out of credit, or its workspace reached the spend limit set in
the Console. Its Ticket is released the same way, and the last line names the
budget but not when access returns, since the human looks at the Console either
way:

  released #6 Rebase conflict resolution · out of API budget at implement

Out of API budget.

When a Ticket a busy Lane held is released too, out of API budget outranks the
rate limit and an API failure, because it alone needs the human to act, and the
rate limit outranks an API failure: a Ticket the limit released afterwards puts
its own last line in place of `API failure.`, with the reset time where a Stage
was told one, because that is the line that says when the next Run can start.
Each `released` row keeps its own cause.

A Ticket whose failing Check or red CI the Base branch fails too is released
the same way, its Fix budget as it was: the pipeline ran the Check commands at
the branch's merge-base with the Base branch, and one of them failed there. Its
row says so in place of the rate limit, and the last line names the Base
branch, the command and the merge-base, shortened to seven characters. The Note
the pipeline posted about it on the standing Notes issue follows the row, as a
Stage's Note does, from the `pipeline`:

  released #6 Rebase conflict resolution · failing Base branch at checks
  noted    #31 comment · from #6 pipeline · The Base branch `main` fails `npm test`.

Base branch `main` fails `npm test` at 1a2b3c4.

A Ticket a Run resumed has no row of its own, released or stranded: it merges,
is handed off, or is released again like any other, and the header already names
the Run that took it.

`skipped` names why a candidate was passed over: `blocked` for one an open
blocker held back all Run, and otherwise the guard reason that kept it from
being claimed — `spec`, `no-criteria` or `body-only-blockers` for Planning a
guard rejected, `claimed` or `not-ready` for an issue that is nobody's to take.
A stranded Ticket is not one of those: it wears this checkout's own Claim, so it
is resumed rather than `skipped` as `claimed`.

A Run given Ticket numbers, `ticket-runner run 12 13 57 99`, has a row for every
one of them. The ones it took end like any other; each one it did not take is
`skipped` with its reason, after the rows of the Tickets it took:

ticket-runner <version> run <runId> · <duration> · <credential>

  merged   #12 Run: drain the Frontier (PR #14)
  skipped  #57 pull-request
  skipped  #99 no-issue
  skipped  #13 blocked

Frontier blocked.

`claimed` is an issue somebody else holds, `not-ready` one not labelled
`ready-for-agent`, a closed one included, `no-issue` a number with no issue
behind it, and `pull-request` a pull request's number. None of them is commented
on. A guard's reason is the guard's, with its warning comment posted once, as on
any Run. `blocked` is a named Ticket an open blocker still held back when the
Run ended, whatever that blocker is; one another named Ticket blocked is taken
once that Ticket merges. The Tickets it was not given have no row at all: the
Run left them as it found them.

`noted` is a Note a Stage made, or the one the pipeline makes about a failing
Base branch, and follows the row of the Ticket whose Stage, or whose Release,
made it. Its number is where the Note went, not where it came from: `comment`
for a Note that reached an issue already there — the Ticket it named, or a
standing Notes issue already open — and `new` for the one Note of a Run that
found no standing Notes issue and opened it. Most of a Run's Notes land on the
same number as `comment`, which is what gathering them on one issue means. The
row shows the Note's summary trimmed to one line; the whole Note is on GitHub.

The last line says why the Run stopped: `Frontier empty.` when nothing is left,
`Frontier blocked.` when every remaining candidate has an open blocker,
`Rate limited.` or `API rate limited.`, with the reset time where the CLI gave
one, `API failure.`, `Out of API budget.`, or
``Base branch `<base>` fails `<command>` at <commit>.`` when a Release ended the
Run, and `Stopped at <hh:mm> · ...`
when a human stopped it. Where Releases differ, the first one's last line
stands, except that out of API budget outranks the rate limit and an API
failure, and the rate limit outranks an API failure.

`billed` is a Stage whose `system/init` event named another `apiKeySource` than
the Run's credential: anything but `none` on a subscription Run, anything but
`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` on an `--api-key` Run. It follows its Ticket's rows, and the
Run's log named it when the Stage came back. A key an `apiKeyHelper` in the
Host's settings supplies is one, which no environment variable removes:

  merged   #3 Run: drain the Frontier (PR #12)
  billed   #3 implement · apiKeySource apiKeyHelper

A Run a Release stopped prints no `skipped  #<n> blocked` rows and no rows for
the Frontier Tickets it never reached: it stopped before it could say a
candidate was held back all Run. The rows its Lanes earned and the last line are
the whole report.

The `blocked` rows of any other Run are read off the last Frontier it computed,
which is the one its final refill asked for. A candidate another Lane unblocked
on the way was taken rather than held back, so it is not among them.

A Run a human stopped takes no further Ticket, and the Lanes busy when the Stop
arrived finish what they hold. Its last line names the clock time the Stop
arrived and the Tickets those Lanes were holding, so the rows above it can be
read as everything the Run had left to do:

ticket-runner <version> run <runId> · <duration> · <credential>

  merged   #3 Run: drain the Frontier (PR #12)
  merged   #6 Rebase conflict resolution (PR #14)

Stopped at 22:07 · finishing #3 #6.

The time is UTC to the minute, which is the clock the run id in the header is
already written in. A Run with no Lane busy when the Stop arrived has nothing to
finish and says so:

Stopped at 22:07 · nothing to finish.

Like a Run a Release stopped, a stopped Run prints no `skipped  #<n> blocked`
rows and no rows for the Tickets it never reached: it stopped before it could
say a candidate was held back all Run. A Stop that reaches a Run a Release had
already stopped leaves the last line the Release's, because that is what
stopped it; the Stop only asked for what was already happening.

A Run given Ticket numbers that a Stop or a Release ended has no row either for
a named Ticket it could still have taken: the last line says why it did not.
Each one nobody could take still has its `skipped` row.
